title: Job Benefits
description: Health insurance, the 401(k) match and paid time off: the pay you don’t see.
wolfLine: Free money on the table is still on the table. Take it.

employee-benefits.definition: Everything a job gives you besides your paycheck: health insurance, retirement money, paid time off and more.
employee-benefits.example: An employer paying $500 a month toward your health insurance.

premium.definition: What you pay to keep insurance active, whether or not you use it.
premium.example: $65 a paycheck for your work health plan.

401k.definition: A retirement account you get through work. Money goes in straight from your paycheck and is invested until you retire.
401k.example: Putting 5% of each paycheck into your company’s 401(k).

employer-match.definition: Money your employer adds to your 401(k) when you put money in yourself.
employer-match.example: 50 cents for every dollar you save, up to 6% of your pay.

vesting.definition: Earning full ownership of your employer’s match over time. Leave too early and you may lose part of it.
vesting.example: 25% of the match becomes yours for each full year you stay.

paid-time-off.definition: Days you’re paid for without working: vacation, sick days and holidays. Often shortened to PTO.
paid-time-off.example: 15 PTO days a year at $200 a day is worth $3,000.

open-enrollment.definition: The window each year, usually a few weeks, when you can choose or change your work benefits.
open-enrollment.example: Every November, pick next year’s health plan and 401(k) rate.

lessons.title: What Benefits Are Worth
lessons.summary: Your pay is more than your paycheck.

steps.title: Pay is more than the paycheck
steps.body:
[[Employee benefits|employee-benefits]] are everything a job gives you besides your paycheck: health insurance, retirement money, paid time off and more.

They’re worth real money, often thousands of dollars a year. Two jobs with the same salary can be worlds apart.

steps.prompt: Benefit or not?
items: Health insurance the company helps pay for

steps.prompt: Your employer pays $500 a month toward your health insurance. What’s that worth over a year?
Two jobs pay $50,000. One includes health insurance, the other doesn’t. Which really pays more?
steps.explain: Thousands of dollars of coverage is real pay, just not in your bank account.

steps.prompt: Benefits can be worth thousands of dollars a year.
steps.explain: Health insurance alone often is.

steps.prompt: Where do you find a job’s benefits?
choices: The offer letter and the benefits guide
steps.explain: Ask for the benefits guide before you accept.

lessons.title: Health Insurance at Work
lessons.summary: What it costs you, and what your employer chips in.

steps.context: A [[premium]] is what you pay to keep insurance active. At work it usually comes out of each paycheck, and your employer often pays a big share too.
steps.prompt: What’s a premium?
choices: What you pay to keep insurance, used or not
steps.explain: You pay it every month, whether or not you see a doctor.

steps.prompt: Your health premium is $65 a paycheck, 26 paychecks a year. What’s the yearly cost to you?
The full plan costs $7,800 a year and you pay $1,690. How much does your employer pay?
Work health insurance premiums are usually taken out before tax.
steps.explain: Another reason work coverage is a good deal.

steps.prompt: Adding a spouse or kids to your plan usually…
steps.explain: More people covered, higher premium.

steps.prompt: You’re young and healthy. Should you skip work health insurance to keep the $65?
choices: No: one accident can cost far more than a year of premiums
steps.explain: A broken leg can cost tens of thousands of dollars without insurance.

lessons.title: The 401(k)
lessons.summary: Retirement saving, straight from your paycheck.

steps.context: A [[401(k)|401k]] is a retirement account you get through work. Money goes in straight from your paycheck, and it’s invested to grow until you retire.
steps.prompt: Where does 401(k) money come from?
steps.explain: It’s taken out before you ever see it.

steps.prompt: Money in a traditional 401(k) goes in before income tax.
steps.explain: That lowers your tax bill today.

steps.prompt: You put in 5% of a $50,000 salary. How much is that a year?
In 2026, what’s the most you can put into a 401(k) yourself (under age 50)?
steps.explain: The IRS sets the limit each year. For 2026 it’s $24,500.

steps.prompt: Why start a 401(k) in your twenties instead of your forties?
choices: Taxes are lower in your forties
steps.explain: Time is the biggest ingredient in growth.

steps.prompt: Taking money out of a 401(k) before age 59½ usually means taxes plus a 10% penalty.
steps.explain: It’s built for retirement, and the rules enforce it.

steps.prompt: A 401(k) is a ___ account you get through work.
steps.explain: Retirement.

lessons.title: The Employer Match
lessons.summary: Free money. Here’s how not to leave it on the table.

steps.context: Many employers add money to your 401(k) when you do. That’s an [[employer match]]. A common one: 50 cents for every dollar you put in, up to 6% of your pay.
steps.prompt: What’s an employer match?
choices: Money your employer adds when you save
steps.explain: It’s extra pay, delivered to your retirement account.

steps.prompt: Salary $50,000. You put in 6% ($3,000), and your employer matches 50% of that. How much do they add?
If you only put in 2% ($1,000), how much would they add?
How much free money do you leave on the table by putting in 2% instead of 6%?
Best move when there’s a match?
choices: Put in at least enough to get the full match
steps.explain: An instant return you can’t get anywhere else.

steps.prompt: A 100% match on your first 4% doubles that money instantly.
steps.explain: Put in $100, and $200 lands in the account.

lessons.title: Lee Leaves Early
lessons.summary: Your match might not be all yours yet. Do the math before you go.

story.title: Leaving money behind
story.body:
Lee put **$6,000** of pay into the company 401(k) over two years. The employer added **$3,000** in matching money.

But the match comes with [[vesting]]: Lee only fully owns it after a set time. This company vests **25%** of the match for every full year worked.

Lee has a new job offer paying **$2,000** a year more, and would leave after exactly **2** years.

steps.prompt: How much of Lee’s own $6,000 can Lee keep?
steps.explain: All of it. Your own contributions are always yours.

steps.prompt: What percent of the match is vested after 2 full years?
How much of the $3,000 match can Lee take?
What’s the total Lee leaves with?
Staying 2 more years would vest the other $1,500. Is leaving still worth it?
choices: Probably: $2,000 more a year beats a one-time $1,500
Only if the new job has no match
steps.explain: $4,000 more pay over two years beats $1,500 of match. Just know the trade-off.

steps.prompt: Your own 401(k) contributions are always 100% yours.
steps.explain: Vesting only applies to the employer’s money.

lessons.title: Paid Time Off
lessons.summary: Days off you’re paid for are worth real money.

steps.context: [[Paid time off|paid-time-off]] (PTO) is days you’re paid for without working: vacation, sick days and holidays.
steps.prompt: What does PTO mean?
choices: Days you’re paid for without working
steps.explain: Vacation, sick days and holidays, paid.

steps.prompt: You earn $25 an hour. One PTO day is 8 hours. What’s it worth?
15 PTO days a year at $200 each. What are they worth?

steps.context: Some companies have “use it or lose it” rules: unused days vanish at the end of the year.
steps.prompt: Your company is use-it-or-lose-it, and you have 5 days left in December. Smart move?
steps.explain: Unused days under that rule are just lost pay.

steps.prompt: Every US employer must give paid vacation.
steps.explain: No federal law requires paid vacation. That’s why it’s worth comparing between offers.

steps.prompt: Same pay. Job A gives 10 PTO days, Job B gives 20. Job B is worth roughly…
choices: 10 extra paid days off a year
steps.explain: Two extra weeks off, paid.

lessons.title: The Benefits Menu
lessons.summary: What each benefit does for you, and what to grab first.

steps.prompt: What does each benefit do for you?
Which benefit should almost everyone take first?
choices: Enough 401(k) to get the full match
steps.explain: Free money comes first.

steps.prompt: Under 26, you can usually stay on a parent’s health plan instead of your job’s.
steps.explain: Compare the costs. Either one can be cheaper.

steps.prompt: A commuter benefit lets you pay your $150 monthly transit pass before tax. At a 22% tax rate, how much does that save a month?
A benefit you’ll never use (pet insurance, and you have no pet) is worth…
choices: Nothing to you, so skip it
steps.explain: Only pick what you’ll use.

steps.context: [[Open enrollment]] is the window each year, usually a few weeks, when you choose or change your benefits.
